claims.text: Forging as-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 at approximately 800 °C followed by partial recrystallization annealing will produce a heterogeneous or gradient grain structure.
The proposed treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation from 13.5% to approximately 20% or more.
The proposed treatment will preserve a yield strength near 786 MPa.
The proposed treatment will preserve impact-triggered chemical energy release.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a terminal strain of 13.5%.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain is indicative of limited tensile ductility and can serve as the baseline uniform tensile elongation.
A heterogeneous grain structure promotes dislocation storage and back-stress hardening.
The thermomechanical treatment will refine the microstructure by creating a bimodal grain-size distribution.
The bimodal or heterogeneous grain structure will enhance dislocation accumulation and delay strain localization during tensile loading.
Delayed strain localization will produce more uniform tensile plastic deformation and greater uniform elongation.
The phase distribution responsible for impact-triggered energy release will remain intact after forging and annealing.
The predicted tensile response applies at room temperature under quasi-static strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The hypothesis is bounded to temperatures from 25 °C to 800 °C under strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats a reported 13.5% terminal strain as though it were uniform tensile elongation, although these are distinct measures and the hypothesis provides no cited basis for equating them.

The predicted target is at least approximately 20% uniform elongation, but the stated ductility falsification threshold is only below approximately 15%. Results between 15% and 20% would miss the prediction without clearly falsifying it.
The conditions place complementary impact tests under similar quasi-static strain-rate conditions, whereas the experimental design calls for dynamic impact tests.
